subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the equation of the parabola passing through the points (−1, 2), (1, −1), (2, 1) and having its axis parallel to the x-axis.

mark_split.label: Set up the general equation and substitute the three points
Eliminate n to get two equations in l and m
Substitute back for n and write the final equation

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Maths-2B, LAQ chapter 2 Parabola — this is the book's own answer 10 (named 'LAQ 10' on the hit list, book p.7: 'Find the equation of the parabola passing through the points (−1,2), (1,−1), (2,1) and having its axis parallel to the x-axis', cross-referenced there as 'Ans-Page P23(10)'). steps.label: Set up the general equation
steps.margin_note: First two marks, for the correct general form and all three substitutions.
lines: with axis parallel to the x-axis is x
steps.why: An axis parallel to the x-axis means y is the free variable and x is written in terms of y², so the general equation has y² and y in place of the usual x² and x — three unknowns l, m, n need three points, which is exactly what is given.
common_mistakes: Writing the general form as y = lx² + mx + n, which is the axis-parallel-to-y-axis case instead.
Substituting a point's x and y into the wrong side of the equation.
steps.memory_tip: Axis along x means x is written in terms of y — x = ly² + my + n, the mirror image of the more familiar y = lx² + mx + n.

steps.label: Eliminate n
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The second subtraction is the shortcut — it hands over m without solving two equations together.
steps.why: Subtracting one equation from another cancels n straight away, since n appears with the same coefficient (1) in every equation — the second subtraction happens to cancel l as well, which is why m comes out immediately.
common_mistakes: Subtracting in the wrong order and losing a sign, e.g. writing 3 = 3l + m instead of −3 = 3l + m.
Forgetting that (2) − (3) also cancels l, and trying to solve for m and l together instead of reading m off directly.
steps.memory_tip: Subtract any equation from a third one and n always leaves first, since every equation has the same +n.

steps.label: Solve for l
steps.margin_note: Two marks for l — this is the step where the earlier fractions have to be carried through carefully.
steps.why: With m already known, (4) has only l left in it, so it is now a one-step equation.
common_mistakes: Losing the 1/2 when moving it to the other side (writing 3l = −3 instead of 3l = −7/2).
Leaving the answer as an improper computation instead of the single fraction −7/6.
steps.memory_tip: m is already known — put it in and (4) is a one-line equation for l.

steps.label: Write the final equation
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Check the boxed equation by putting one of the three given points back in — it should give 0.
lines: n = 8/3 in x = ly² + my + n:
steps.why: Multiplying through by 6, the least common denominator of 6, 2 and 3, clears every fraction in one move and leaves a whole-number equation — the standard way to present a final locus.
common_mistakes: Multiplying only some of the terms by 6 and leaving a mixed equation.
Writing the boxed equation with a wrong sign on the y term.
steps.memory_tip: Multiply the whole equation by the smallest number that clears every denominator at once — here that number is 6.

insider_note: This method mirrors answer 12 in this same chapter exactly, with x and y swapped — learn one and the other follows for free. The examiner is checking the elimination of n first, since that is the step most students rush.
